items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Workers are faking their interest in AI to satisfy bosses, report shows
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Corporate leaders are putting tremendous pressure on workers to incorporate artificial intelligence into their workflow—often without a clear understanding of its capabilities or impact. As a result, some employees are simply faking their usage of AI. 

According to a new report by Vancouver-based software firm Visier, nearly half of workers (48%) said they have “exaggerated their AI usage or expertise to colleagues or leadership” to keep up with expectations. 

Visier polled 1,000 full-time workers in the United States—across healthcare, finance, human resources, and other domains—about how they use AI and their opinion on their firm’s AI strategy. 

The survey found that while AI has had a real impact on many workers—54% of respondents said their roles or careers had “significantly changed due to AI in the past two years”—the nature of its impact varied widely from worker to worker. Some said AI has improved their job performance and satisfaction, while others reported that its impact was mostly negative. 

Anxiety and uncertainty caused by AI were widespread. Nearly 60% said they are unsure of their employer’s plan to address changes brought on by AI, and 45% said they felt pressured to use AI “even when they’re not confident in how to use it effectively.”

The pressure to use AI leads some workers to pretend they are using it even when they aren’t, believing that showing enthusiasm for AI matters just as much (or more than) getting better results. 

Indeed, the report concludes that the underlying driver of “performative AI use” is a lack of trust in leadership. Nearly a third (32%) of respondents told Visier they want “more AI training and upskilling opportunities,” while 31% called for “greater transparency” on AI-related issues. 

Simply telling workers to “have AI do it” isn’t going to cut it—they must be told how. Along with resisting the pull of AI FOMO, leaders should listen to employees’ concerns, stay transparent about how AI might affect their work, and provide the necessary training. 

“By providing employees with opportunities to upskill, learn, and share knowledge among colleagues, leaders can proactively prevent performative AI behaviors and help alleviate workforce anxiety,” the report states.

items.title: 🔓 [Macworld] Best iPhone 2026: Every iPhone compared
items.content_html:
Macworld

Apple’s 2026 iPhone lineup is broader than ever, ranging from the relatively affordable iPhone 17e to the high-end iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, plus the ultra-thin iPhone Air and the new folding iPhone Duo. That gives buyers more choice, but it also makes picking the right model more complicated than simply choosing the newest or most expensive iPhone.

For most people, the iPhone 17 is the best all-round choice, thanks to its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, strong battery life, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage as standard. The iPhone 17e is the better option if price matters most, while the iPhone 18 Pro is the model to choose for the best cameras and performance. The iPhone 18 Pro Max adds the longest battery life, the iPhone Air prioritises thinness and low weight, and the iPhone Duo offers Apple’s biggest and most flexible display.

Which iPhone is best for you will therefore depend on what you value most. Camera enthusiasts should look closely at the Pro models, heavy users may prefer the Pro Max for its battery life, while parents, older users and anyone trying to keep costs down may find the 17e a much better fit. There can also be excellent value in buying a discounted or refurbished older iPhone rather than paying full price for the latest hardware.

This guide focuses on the best iPhone to buy for different types of user and budget. If you want to dig deeper into the differences between every model, see our complete iPhone Buying Guide, where we compare the cameras, displays, performance, storage, battery life and other key specifications across Apple’s current lineup.

Which iPhone to buy: At a glance

1. Apple iPhone 17 – Best iPhone for most people

Pros

  • Excellent overall value
  • ProMotion Always-On display
  • Dual 48MP cameras

Cons

  • No dedicated telephoto
  • Limited to 512GB

Why we recommend it

The iPhone 17 brings several features previously reserved for Pro models to Apple’s mainstream iPhone, including a 120Hz ProMotion display and Always-On support. It also offers the fast A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras, an improved Centre Stage selfie camera, strong battery life and 256GB of storage as standard. For most buyers, it strikes the best balance between price and features.

Buy iPhone 17 if

Buy the iPhone 17 if you want the best all-round iPhone without paying Pro prices. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion display, excellent cameras, strong battery life and 256GB starting storage make it particularly appealing to anyone upgrading from an iPhone 14 or older.

Don’t buy iPhone 17 if

Don’t buy it if you want optical zoom beyond 2x or Apple’s most advanced camera features—in that case, choose the iPhone 18 Pro. The iPhone Air is a better choice if thinness and low weight are your priorities, while existing iPhone 16 owners may find the upgrade relatively modest unless ProMotion and improved battery life are particularly important.

What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 17e?

For the extra $200, the iPhone 17 gives you a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, Dynamic Island, a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera with macro photography, a brighter screen, stronger graphics performance, a better 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera and longer battery life. For most people who can afford the difference, it’s money well spent.

What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 16?

For $100 more, you get double the base storage at 256GB, a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, an upgraded 48MP Ultra Wide camera, an improved 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera, longer battery life, faster charging and the newer A19 processor. At full price, the iPhone 17 is the better buy.

Key specs

The iPhone 17 combines a 6.3-inch ProMotion display, Always-On support and the A19 chip with dual 48MP rear cameras and 256GB of storage as standard. It offers many of the features most people actually want from a Pro iPhone without the Pro price.

  • Starts at: $799 / £799 (256GB)
  • Display: 6.3-inch OLED ProMotion (120Hz)
  • Chip: A19
  • Storage: 256GB–512GB
  • Cameras: 48MP Main + 48MP Ultra Wide, 18MP front camera
  • Battery: Up to 30 hours of video playback

Should you buy or wait?

Buy now. The iPhone 17 offers excellent value, while the iPhone 18 isn’t expected until spring 2027 and may bring higher prices rather than transformative upgrades. Waiting for Prime Day or Black Friday could make sense if you’re looking for a discount.

Read our full Apple iPhone 17 review

2. Apple iPhone 18 Pro – Best for photography

Pros

  • Excellent triple-camera system
  • Powerful A20 Pro chip
  • Strong battery life

Cons

  • Expensive starting price
  • Overkill for most buyers

Why we recommend it

The iPhone 18 Pro is the model to buy if you want Apple’s best cameras and performance without stepping up to the much larger Pro Max or experimental folding iPhone Duo. Its variable-aperture camera will be a meaningful upgrade for some photographers – although our reviewer found the practical effect modest and valued the manual controls more. The A20 Pro chip, improved cooling, longer battery life and faster charging make it particularly capable for gaming, video and demanding AI workloads. Crucially, it gets the same cameras and processor as the Pro Max, making it the better-value Pro model for most buyers.

Buy iPhone 18 Pro if

Buy the iPhone 18 Pro if you want Apple’s best camera system; need more performance than the standard iPhone offers; regularly play demanding games or use intensive creative or AI apps; or want excellent battery life without carrying the enormous Pro Max. It’s a compelling upgrade for anyone with an iPhone 15 Pro or older.

Don’t buy iPhone 18 Pro if

Most people don’t need the iPhone 18 Pro. The standard iPhone 17 already offers an excellent 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display, A19 chip, dual 48MP cameras, 256GB of storage and strong battery life for considerably less. And if your main priority is screen size and endurance, the Pro Max is the better choice.

What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 17?

The biggest advantage is the camera system. The iPhone 18 Pro adds a 48MP Telephoto camera with 4x and 8x optical-quality zoom, plus a variable-aperture 48MP Main camera for improved low-light shooting and greater creative control. You also get the faster A20 Pro chip with a seven-core GPU and improved vapor-chamber cooling for better sustained performance during gaming, video editing and AI tasks.

Key specs

The iPhone 18 Pro combines Apple’s new 2nm A20 Pro processor with a sophisticated triple-48MP camera system, including a variable-aperture Main camera and 4x/8x Telephoto. It retains a manageable 6.3-inch ProMotion display while improving sustained performance, battery life and charging speeds.

  • Starts at: $1,199 / £1,199 (256GB)
  • Display: 6.3-inch OLED ProMotion (120Hz)
  • Chip: A20 Pro, 6-core CPU, 7-core GPU
  • Storage: 256GB–2TB
  • Cameras: 48MP variable-aperture Main + 48MP Ultra Wide + 48MP Telephoto (4x/8x), 18MP front camera
  • Battery: Up to 36 hours of video playback

Should you buy or wait?

The iPhone 18 Pro is available now. Buy it if you want the Pro camera system and performance in a smaller phone – the Pro Max offers the same cameras. Bargain hunters may prefer to hold off until Amazon’s Prime Day sale in October, or Black Friday on November 27, when retailers and mobile networks may offer trade-in bonuses, contract incentives or modest discounts. Large outright savings are unlikely so soon after launch.

Read our full Apple iPhone 18 Pro review

Why we recommend it

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple’s ultimate conventional iPhone, combining a huge 6.9-inch ProMotion display with the powerful A20 Pro chip, Apple’s best camera system and the longest battery life in the range. Its biggest advantage over the regular Pro is endurance, with Apple rating it for up to 45 hours of video playback.

Our testing backs up the battery recommendation: the iPhone 18 Pro Max lasted 25 percent longer than the iPhone 17 Pro Max in our Geekbench 4 battery test, with screen brightness fixed at 200 nits. This is a separate measurement from Apple’s video-playback rating and provides another reason to choose the Pro Max if endurance is your priority.

Buy the iPhone 18 Pro Max if

Buy the iPhone 18 Pro Max if you want the biggest possible display and longest battery life, regularly use your phone for photography, video, gaming or other demanding tasks, and don’t mind carrying a large and relatively heavy device. It’s particularly well suited to frequent travellers and heavy users who want to minimise charging.

Don’t buy iPhone 18 Pro Max if

Don’t buy it if you prefer a smaller, lighter phone or simply want the Pro cameras and performance. The iPhone 18 Pro offers essentially the same A20 Pro chip, camera system and Pro features in a more manageable 6.3-inch design for $100/£100 less. At 249g, the Pro Max is also particularly heavy.

What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 18 Pro?

Not much in terms of features. Both models have the same A20 Pro processor, triple-48MP camera system, variable-aperture Main camera and storage options up to 2TB. The Pro Max instead gives you a larger 6.9-inch display rather than 6.3 inches and substantially better battery life: up to 45 hours of video playback versus 36 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro. You pay an extra $100/£100 for those advantages.

Key specs

The iPhone 18 Pro Max combines Apple’s huge 6.9-inch ProMotion display with the new 2nm A20 Pro chip, three 48MP rear cameras and a variable-aperture Main camera. Its defining advantage is battery life, reaching up to 45 hours of video playback.

  • Starts at: $1,299 / £1,299 (256GB)
  • Display: 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR OLED ProMotion (120Hz)
  • Chip: A20 Pro, 6-core CPU, 7-core GPU
  • Storage: 256GB–2TB
  • Cameras: 48MP variable-aperture Main + 48MP Ultra Wide + 48MP Telephoto, 18MP front camera
  • Battery: Up to 45 hours of video playback

Should you buy or wait?

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is available now. Choose it over the smaller Pro if longer battery life and a larger display justify the extra cost and weight. If your current phone lasts comfortably through the day, there is less urgency to upgrade, and waiting for a discount could make sense. Compare the total cost of carrier offers and trade-ins with buying outright. Bargain hunters may prefer to wait for Amazon’s Prime Day sales in October or Black Friday on November 27. Major outright discounts are unlikely so soon after launch, although trade-in offers and contract incentives could be worthwhile.

4. Apple iPhone Duo – Best foldable iPhone

Pros

  • Innovative folding displayExcellent multitasking potentialStrong A20 Pro performance

Why we recommend it

The iPhone Duo offers something no other iPhone can: a compact phone that unfolds into a 7.6-inch tablet-like device. The larger display gives you considerably more room for multitasking, watching video, reading, gaming and creative work, while the outer screen keeps it usable as a conventional phone when closed. Add the A20 Pro chip and clever dual-screen features and it’s easily Apple’s most innovative iPhone.

Buy iPhone Duo if

Buy the iPhone Duo if you want the versatility of an iPhone and small tablet in one device, regularly multitask between apps, consume lots of content on your phone, or simply want Apple’s most distinctive new hardware. It’s particularly compelling if you value screen space and flexibility more than having Apple’s absolute best camera system.

Don’t buy iPhone Duo if

Don’t buy the Duo if value, photography or portability are your priorities. At $1,999/£1,999 it costs $800/£800 more than the iPhone 18 Pro, while lacking Face ID, a dedicated telephoto camera, variable aperture, ProRes and the Action button. At 254g it is also the heaviest iPhone in the range. For most buyers, the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max will be a better all-round purchase.

What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max?

The Duo’s defining advantage is its 7.6-inch folding display, which offers around 50 percent more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max and supports Split View multitasking, while the 5.4-inch outer screen keeps it usable like a compact iPhone when closed. You also get fold-specific features such as Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue, hands-free video positioning and an under-display inner camera, with Apple Pencil USB-C support coming later in 2026. The trade-off is photography: the Duo has only two 48MP rear cameras, with no dedicated telephoto, variable aperture, ProRes or Apple Log.

Key specs

The iPhone Duo transforms from a compact 5.4-inch phone into a 7.6-inch folding device, providing substantially more room for apps, video and multitasking. It combines two 120Hz ProMotion OLED displays with the A20 Pro chip, dual 48MP cameras, strong battery life and storage up to 2TB.

  • Starts at: $1,999 / £1,999 (256GB)
  • Displays: 5.4-inch outer + 7.6-inch folding OLED, ProMotion (120Hz)
  • Chip: A20 Pro
  • Storage: 256GB–2TB
  • Cameras: 48MP Main + 48MP Ultra Wide, 12MP outer front camera + under-display inner camera
  • Battery: Up to 44 hours of video playback on outer display; 31 hours on inner display
  • Authentication: Touch ID
  • Weight: 254g

Should you buy or wait?

The iPhone Duo goes on sale October 23, with pre-orders opening October 16. Buy at launch if you want Apple’s first foldable as soon as possible. If price matters more than being first, waiting until Black Friday on November 27 could bring carrier incentives or trade-in deals, although significant outright discounts on such a new and specialised device are unlikely.

The iPhone 17e is Apple’s most affordable current iPhone, offering modern performance and Apple Intelligence without flagship pricing. It combines the A19 chip with useful upgrades including MagSafe and 256GB of base storage. If you don’t need multiple cameras or a high-refresh-rate display, it delivers the essentials at an attractive price.

Buy the iPhone 17e if

Buy the iPhone 17e if you want a modern iPhone with strong performance and years of software support for as little as possible. It’s particularly appealing to anyone upgrading from an iPhone 12 or 13, switching from Android or buying their first iPhone.

Don’t buy iPhone 17e if

Don’t buy it if you want ProMotion, an Always-On display, Dynamic Island or a versatile camera system. If your budget stretches another $200/£200, the iPhone 17 is a substantially more complete phone.

What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 16?

The iPhone 17e gives you the newer A19 chip, longer battery life, 256GB of storage as standard, Apple’s newer C1X modem and Ceramic Shield 2 protection. Its biggest advantage, however, is value: at similar real-world prices, it is generally the smarter long-term purchase.

What don’t you get that you get with the iPhone 17?

The iPhone 17 gives you a larger and significantly more advanced 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display with Dynamic Island and Always-On support, plus a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera. You also get a better 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera, stronger graphics performance and longer battery life. The 17e covers the essentials extremely well, but the iPhone 17 feels much more complete.

Key specs

The iPhone 17e pairs the A19 chip with a 6.1-inch OLED display, 256GB of storage as standard and up to 26 hours of battery life, while omitting premium features such as Dynamic Island, ProMotion and an Ultra Wide camera.

Should you buy or wait?

Buy now. The iPhone 17e offers excellent value and isn’t expected to be replaced until early 2027. Discounts could make it even more attractive, but there’s little reason to delay purely for the next generation.

The iPhone Air’s biggest advantage is its exceptionally thin and light titanium design. You also get a slightly larger 6.5-inch display, the more powerful A19 Pro chip and storage options up to 1TB.   • Storage: 128GB–512GB
  • Cameras: 48MP Main + 12MP Ultra Wide
  • Battery: Up to 22 hours of video playback

Should you buy or wait?

Don’t buy at full price. Only consider the iPhone 16 if it’s heavily discounted below the iPhone 17e; otherwise, Apple’s newer models offer substantially better value.

Read our full Apple iPhone 16 review

Which iPhone has the best camera? iPhone 18 Pro

Apple

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have the best camera systems of any current iPhone. Both models use the same triple-48MP rear camera setup, so there is no photographic advantage to choosing the larger Pro Max unless you also want its bigger display and longer battery life.

The headline upgrade is the 48MP Main camera with variable aperture, which gives photographers more control over depth of field and should improve low-light performance. The Pro models also include a 48MP Ultra Wide camera and a 48MP Telephoto camera with 4x and 8x optical-quality zoom, giving them far more flexibility than Apple’s cheaper iPhones.

The standard iPhone 17 is still an excellent camera phone, with 48MP Main and Ultra Wide cameras, plus an improved 18MP Centre Stage front camera. For everyday photography it will be more than enough for most people, but it lacks the dedicated telephoto lens, longer zoom and advanced video features of the Pro models.

The iPhone Duo is more compromised. Despite its premium price, it has only two 48MP rear cameras and lacks a dedicated telephoto camera, variable aperture, ProRes and Apple Log. Its strengths are instead its fold-specific shooting features and dual-screen flexibility.

The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e are the least versatile, with just a single 48MP rear camera.

Our choice: If photography and video are your priority, buy the iPhone 18 Pro. It offers the same camera system as the Pro Max for less money and in a more manageable size.

Which iPhone has the best battery life? iPhone 18 Pro Max

Apple

The iPhone 18 Pro Max has the best battery life of any current iPhone, with Apple rating it for up to 45 hours of video playback. That puts it comfortably ahead of the smaller iPhone 18 Pro and makes battery life one of the strongest reasons to choose the Pro Max.

The iPhone Duo comes surprisingly close, with up to 44 hours of video playback when using its outer 5.4-inch display. However, battery life drops to around 31 hours when using the larger 7.6-inch folding display, so the Pro Max remains the better choice if endurance is your priority.

The iPhone 18 Pro is also excellent, offering up to 36 hours of video playback. That makes it a good compromise if you want strong battery life without carrying the much larger and heavier Pro Max.

Further down the range, the iPhone 17 offers up to 30 hours, making it the best mainstream option for battery life. The iPhone Air manages around 27 hours despite its exceptionally thin design, while the iPhone 17e reaches 26 hours.

The older iPhone 16 trails the current lineup at up to 22 hours of video playback.

Our choice: If battery life matters above everything else, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the clear winner. Its combination of a 45-hour rating, huge 6.9-inch display and Pro-level performance makes it particularly well suited to heavy users, travellers and anyone who wants to get through a long day without worrying about charging.

Here’s how the current iPhone lineup compares in terms of battery life

What is the best value iPhone? iPhone 17

Hannah Cowton-Barnes / Foundry

The iPhone 17 offers the best overall value for money in Apple’s current lineup. The iPhone 17e is cheaper, but the extra $200/£200 for the iPhone 17 buys a surprisingly large number of worthwhile upgrades.

You get a larger 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display with Always-On support and Dynamic Island, rather than the 17e’s standard 60Hz 6.1-inch screen. The iPhone 17 also adds a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera, including macro photography, along with a better 18MP Centre Stage front camera.

Battery life is stronger too, at up to 30 hours of video playback, compared with 26 hours on the iPhone 17e. You also get stronger graphics performance and a more premium overall experience, while both phones start with a generous 256GB of storage.

At $799/£799, the iPhone 17 also compares very favourably with the older iPhone 16. For just $100/£100 more, you get double the base storage, ProMotion, a larger and brighter display, improved cameras, the newer A19 chip and significantly better battery life.

If your priority is spending as little as possible, choose the iPhone 17e which delivers excellent performance for $599/£599. Or seek out a refurbished iPhone from the Apple Refurbished Store or another place that sells refurbished iPhones.

Our choice: In terms of the features and hardware you get for every pound or dollar spent, the iPhone 17 is the sweet spot. For most buyers, it delivers the best balance of price, performance, cameras, display quality, battery life and longevity without paying for Pro-level features they may never use. Even better if you can find a iPhone 17 deal, then you are really getting a bargain.

Best iPhone for gaming: iPhone 18 Pro

Foundry

The iPhone 18 Pro is the best iPhone for gaming for most people, thanks to its combination of the A20 Pro chip, seven-core GPU and improved vapor-chamber cooling.

The A20 Pro is Apple’s fastest iPhone processor, but the cooling system is just as important for gaming. Better heat management should help the iPhone 18 Pro maintain high performance for longer during demanding games, rather than slowing down as the phone gets hot. Its 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display also provides smooth animation and responsive gameplay without making the phone excessively large or heavy.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers essentially the same gaming performance, but adds a much larger 6.9-inch display and significantly longer battery life. That arguably makes it the best choice for serious mobile gamers who value screen size and endurance, although it is heavier and costs more.

The iPhone Duo also uses the A20 Pro and has an enormous 7.6-inch folding display, which could be fantastic for some games, but its weight, price and unconventional form factor make it a more specialised choice.

Our choice: For most gamers, the iPhone 18 Pro offers the best balance of performance, cooling, display quality and portability. It’s the best choice if you prefer a more pocketable device but still want top-tier gaming power.

Best iPhone for seniors and older users: iPhone 17e

David Price / Foundry

For most older users, the iPhone 17e is probably the best choice, because it combines a relatively simple feature set with modern performance, strong battery life and a lower price than Apple’s flagship models.

Its 6.1-inch OLED display is large enough to make text, icons and controls easy to see without making the phone too bulky, while the A19 chip should keep it feeling fast for years. It also supports Apple Intelligence and starts with 256GB of storage, so there’s plenty of room for photos, apps and videos.

The iPhone 17 is a better option for someone who would benefit from a larger and more advanced display. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion screen, Always-On support and higher brightness can make scrolling, reading and outdoor use more comfortable. It also offers stronger battery life and better cameras, although it costs more.

We don’t recommend the iPhone Air, Pro Max or Duo for older users. The Air sacrifices battery life and camera flexibility for thinness, while the Pro Max and Duo are much heavier and considerably more expensive.

Our choice: iPhone 17e is the perfect choice for most older users.

Best iPhone for kids: iPhone 17e

Ida Blix

The iPhone 17e is the best iPhone for most children. As Apple’s most affordable current-generation model, it offers the best balance of price, performance and longevity, while being easier to justify than a flagship model if it gets lost or damaged.

It uses the same A19 chip as the iPhone 17, albeit with one fewer GPU core, so it’s easily fast enough for games, social media, schoolwork and Apple Intelligence. Battery life is strong, the 6.1-inch OLED display is a sensible size for smaller hands, and the 48MP camera is more than capable for everyday photos, even though it lacks an Ultra Wide lens.

The iPhone 17 is the better choice for older teenagers who care more about photography, video or display quality. It adds a 48MP Ultra Wide camera, a better front camera and a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion display, but costs considerably more.

A hand-me-down iPhone is also worth considering. It’s the cheapest option and better for the environment, provided you erase the phone first, create a Child Account through Family Sharing, and configure Screen Time and parental controls before handing it over. Read: How to set up an iPhone for a child.

Whichever iPhone you choose, those controls matter. In iOS 27, Apple is expanding Screen Time with new category-based Time Allowances, Ask to Browse, more flexible app schedules and improved contact controls. Communication Safety can also detect and blur sensitive, violent or graphic content.

For very young children, an iPad may still be a better first Apple device. By the time they reach 11 or 12 though, an iPhone becomes much more useful for staying in touch.

Our choice: iPhone 17e for most kids; iPhone 17 for older teens who want better cameras and display quality.

Should you buy an older iPhone?

Macwelt

Buying an older iPhone can be a great way to save money, but the key is choosing a model that still has plenty of useful life ahead of it. Apple typically provides around five to seven years of major iOS updates, with security updates often continuing for longer, so a relatively recent iPhone can remain perfectly usable for years.

We wouldn’t recommend simply buying the cheapest iPhone you can find. Very old models may technically run recent versions of iOS, but performance, battery condition and access to newer features can become increasingly compromised. We currently recommend avoiding anything older than the iPhone 15 Pro because even the iPhone 15 doesn’t support Apple Intelligence. You should definitely avoid models such as the iPhone XS and XR that can no longer run the latest iOS releases.

A refurbished recent-generation iPhone can offer particularly good value. You may be able to buy a former Pro model with better cameras and displays for less than a new entry-level iPhone. Buying from a reputable refurbisher is important, however: check the warranty, battery condition, returns policy and whether genuine replacement parts have been used. Apple’s own refurbished iPhones include a new battery and outer shell and come with a one-year warranty.

Our advice: A discounted or refurbished iPhone 16 or newer should offer an excellent combination of price, features and longevity.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Entry-level tech jobs in NYC are being cut in half by the AI boom
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

🪶 ✏️

🪶 ✏️

At first glance, the tech scene in New York City appears to be thriving: OpenAI and Anthropic have been putting down roots in the city, while stalwarts of the tech industry like Google now have more than 14,000 employees based in New York. Between 2008 and 2023, tech employment in the city has increased 160%, outdone only by the explosive growth of the tech industry in San Francisco.

But overall job growth in NYC’s tech industry has stagnated in recent years, and there is one area in particular that has experienced a sharp dip: Entry-level tech jobs have taken a significant hit in the years since ChatGPT’s public release ushered in the AI boom. 

A new report from the Center for an Urban Future (CUF), a New York-based think tank, found that as of 2022, the number of entry-level job postings in the tech industry has dropped 49%—a bigger decline than in any other sector, even as generative AI has seemingly derailed entry-level hiring across sectors. There continues to be a steady supply of college graduates with computer science degrees, but there aren’t nearly enough entry-level positions available to them. 

“The core issue is that employers face an individual incentive to hire workers who already have two or three years of experience,” Eli Dvorkin, editorial and policy director at CUF and one of the authors of the report, said in a recent interview with Searchlight. “But if every employer acts that way, the broader entry-level ecosystem collapses, which ultimately harms employers as well.”

The analysis found that on the whole, the jobs that have seen a marked dip in hiring are those that are most exposed to generative AI. Since 2022, entry-level job postings in roles with high AI exposure have decreased 29% across New York City. 

The outlook is not quite as grim across other jobs: Entry-level hiring has remained robust—growing 21%—for jobs that are not especially exposed to AI, according to the CUF report. Even within tech, employers have continued hiring for roles that require expertise in security and data analysis. Entry-level workers with strong AI skills are in particularly high demand, and job postings have actually climbed 20% in over the past four years. 

Still, the overall decline in hiring for entry-level tech jobs echoes a broader shift in New York: Since 2022, most industries have seen a steady drop in job postings for entry-level roles. 

This hiring slump is representative of a broader phenomenon playing out across the country, particularly in sectors like tech and finance. Some economists have been wary about overstating the impact of generative AI on the labor force—and even high-profile AI leaders have walked back their bold claims about AI ushering in widespread job losses. 

But there are clear signs that entry-level workers are bearing the brunt of the toll: Stanford University’s Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence recently found that the employment gap for young workers (defined as workers ages 22 to 25) has widened in the last year to 19%, when compared against similarly situated workers in roles that are less exposed to AI. 

In a recent survey by the Pew Research Center, young workers were more skeptical of AI than they had been previously, a sign that they are increasingly concerned about how the fast-developing technology might upend the labor market. Nearly three-quarters of adults younger than 30 said they believe AI will reduce the number of jobs within the next two decades.

The reports of looming job losses often focus on how generative AI is impacting white-collar workers, but research from the Brookings Institution earlier this year indicates that it’s not just highly skilled candidates who are being shut out of the workforce. AI adoption is also disrupting the pathways available to people without college degrees who have traditionally been able to move into white-collar work. 

In cities like New York, the growth in tech employment has in the past helped many workers from low-income backgrounds move into more lucrative jobs—but the changes ushered in by AI may make it more difficult for those types of workers to find their footing. Those pathways could disappear altogether if the city doesn’t reinvest in its tech workforce and help New Yorkers get the experience they need to land the entry-level jobs that are in high demand. 

As Dvorkin put it recently: “If anything, our tech sector has proven remarkably resilient given all these macroeconomic changes and technology shifts, and it remains well-positioned for future growth. However, the real challenge is who gets the opportunity to enter that sector in the first place.”

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Executives are using AI to communicate better. There’s just one problem
items.content_html:
Artificial intelligence can help executives communicate more effectively and efficiently. But relying on it too much carries significant risks. 

One of the biggest is something Wade Foster, cofounder and chief executive of workflow automation platform Zapier, calls the “comprehension gap”—failing to adequately understand the underlying subject matter of their own AI-assisted work. 

Leaders who overuse AI to write polished memos, emails, or talking points may find themselves unable to answer follow-up questions or back up their claims in real time. The fact that they used AI to create the original material might quickly become obvious. 

“There are definitely situations [where] you don’t use AI responsibly, where you’re delegating too much,” Foster said in an appearance on Harvard Business Review’s IdeaCast earlier today.  

“As you get asked questions, as you start to investigate, you realize, ‘Oh, I don’t actually know enough about this area,’” he said. 

AI overuse can also rob executives of knowledge they would have gained by producing the materials themselves, added Matt Abrahams, a lecturer in organizational behavior at Stanford Graduate School of Business. Composing an internal memo about a regulatory issue, for example, might give an executive a deeper understanding of the issue itself. 

“Communication is operationalized critical thinking,” Abrahams said on the IdeaCast podcast. “If we outsource that critical thinking and then are put on the spot to answer questions, to give input, to give an update, people get really anxious.” 

The key to avoiding such a scenario is to take time studying the AI-generated material until you really comprehend it, Abrahams said. It’s about truly knowing the subject matter, even if you had some help putting the verbiage together.

“It is really important not just to review the output, but to really review the thinking so that when you’re put on the spot, you have the confidence that you know what you’re speaking about,” he said. Otherwise, workers might come to believe that their leaders aren’t doing their homework. 

The business community is still figuring how to responsibly incorporate AI into communications, Foster added. “AI is a fantastic tool, and to not use it would be a mistake. [But] it could be a lot better if you use it responsibly. [That] is what everyone’s trying to figure out.” 

Leaders who overuse AI without understanding the underlying subject matter risk their own credibility—one recent study found that employees view executive communications as less helpful when they think they’re AI-generated (even when they aren’t)—and set a bad example for workers who may be eager to outsource their own work to AI.   

In the end, it may be that there are no hard-and-fast rules for responsible AI use in executive communications. Leaders will have to decide on a case-by-case basis. 

“It just depends on the task,” Foster said. “There could be areas where the impact is relatively low, and you’re fine delegating the work to the AI more fully. 

“It just comes down to judgment.”

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] As the coding boom fades, AI is forcing colleges and computer science grads to adjust
items.content_html:
Computer science student Jack Zemke was getting nowhere despite sending out hundreds of job applications that mostly disappeared into the void—ignored.

With his graduation from Tulane University just days away, he was considering moving back in with his parents when he got a break, thanks to a group project he had worked on involving an AI-powered search tool. As he touted it at an engineering conference, an employee at a civil engineering firm approached.

“We’re not, like, the most on top of trends, but we know that AI is becoming a big thing,” he recalled the man saying. “We need somebody to be essentially an evangelist.”

Zemke responded: “I’m your man.”

It has been a difficult job market for new graduates, especially in fields like software development where artificial intelligence is shouldering more of the work. While college students majoring in computer science during the recent coding boom were getting job offers without even applying, graduates today in philosophy, art history, and ethnic studies majors all have higher employment rates.

But as the job market evolves with AI and entry-level jobs become harder to find, students and schools are adapting. Colleges are experimenting with business-specific internships and bolstering training in AI tools. Schools say most graduates ultimately are getting jobs, although increasingly, the employers hiring aren’t tech giants but smaller businesses looking for help figuring out what to do with AI.

Such was the case with Zemke, 23, who spent a year at the engineering firm before getting hired this summer at an AI tech startup.

“These jobs are expecting you to be able to jump in and kind of operate on the frontier,” Zemke said. “There’s so much churn. People are getting laid off. People are leaving. It really feels like a total frenzy right now.”

A coding boom that enticed many students has fizzled

The elevated jobless rate in the field—at around 7.1% for recent computer science and computer engineering graduates, according to an Associated Press analysis—reflects in part the huge numbers of students who enrolled during the coding boom.

Hiring surged during the pandemic as everything went digital, with software development postings on the job search site Indeed peaking in early 2022.

But now tech giants like Microsoft, Meta, and Google are turning to AI for a larger share of the code writing, and big employers like Amazon are shedding workers as spending on AI accelerates. Far fewer jobs in software development are being posted, according to a Federal Reserve analysis of the Indeed data.

For workers in their early 20s in what are being called “AI-exposed” occupations—such as software development—employment is 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with employment in fields less exposed to being reshaped by AI, according to the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. The U.S. Census Bureau likened the employment decline to finishing college during a large recession.

What the industry is demanding now is workers who can oversee AI tools and not blindly accept their outputs—skills more common in seasoned workers, said Tracy Camp, the Computing Research Association’s executive director and CEO.

The effect on hiring of young workers is so concerning that the association has reached out to industry leaders, urging them to invest in entry-level workers.

“If they don’t change how hiring is currently happening, they’re not going to have mid-level career people in a few years,” Camp said.

Students also are taking note. After a decade that saw the number of recent computer science and computer engineering graduates triple, to about 362,000 in 2024, enrollment began to drop last year. The latest data from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center shows that by spring this year, computer and information science enrollment has fallen by 8.4% at four-year institutions.

A shift in hiring disadvantages international students

For international students, who have enrolled in high numbers in computer science programs, it has been an especially challenging job market. Their struggles owe partly to changes to U.S. immigration policy as well as the shift in the kinds of available jobs.

Samir Khuller, the chair of Northwestern University’s computer science department, said many of the smaller companies that are hiring don’t have big human resources departments with experience handling H-1B work visas.

International students generally need an H-1B work visa to stay in the U.S., which requires sponsorship from an employer. The program has become a target of the Trump administration, which is seeking to raise the fee for the visas to over $100,000.

Computer science graduate Collins Kibet, from Kenya, has sent out hundreds of applications and landed just a handful of interviews—mostly with AI bots. The Southern New Hampshire University graduate said that during the rare job interview with a person, the tone shifts when employers learn they would have to sponsor his H-1B work visa.

“Everybody just keeps quiet,” said Kibet, who started his own software company because he could not find a job.

Colleges are rethinking training for computer science students

Watching students navigate job searches has been hard for Nicholas Mattei, an associate computer science professor at Tulane. When he looks at some of the job ads, he thinks, “Really?”

“All the companies are coming back to us and saying, ‘Oh, well you need to train these people even better, and they need to be able to jump into a middle management role as opposed to an introductory or junior developer role,’” he said. “And it’s kind of crazy.”

Many colleges are retooling their computer science programs. With entry-level jobs going away, they are tasked with preparing students to do more.

To give students a leg up, professors at Georgia Tech researched what AT&T wanted and trained students for a month before they started internships with the company. The school plans to expand the effort for a program it will call “Bootcamp to Industry,” said Fisayo Omojokun, the associate dean for undergraduate education in the school’s College of Computing.

Staff tasked with recruiting businesses for College of Computing job fairs are also reaching out to a broader range of industries.

“Earlier this year, we got a call from a forestry company of all things,’” Omojokun said. “They’re like, ‘Hey, we are in forestry, and we know that AI can help in what we do in different ways.’”

The Associated Press’s education coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. AP is solely responsible for all content. Find AP’s standards for working with philanthropies, a list of supporters and funded coverage areas at AP.org.

—By Heather Hollingsworth and Nicky Forster, Associated Press

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Trump administration attacks Australia's 'opt-out' algorithm law in rare intervention
items.content_html:
Cam Wilson, Sept 23, 2026

The U.S. government "wants US social media companies excluded from digital duty of care laws, which would give Australians the option to opt out of algorithmic feeds." Why would this matter? The algorithm is the difference between a social networking service that connects users with people and resources they want and a social networking service that is a channel for advertising and political messaging. Obviously there's a lot more money to be made by the latter, but it also causes a lot of harm. The public interest and social education are fulfilled much better by the former. At some point, instead of simply banning social media for children, people need to have the right to define and build their own algorithms, serving their own interests, without corporate and political interests intervening in the process.

items.content_html:
Simon Willison, Simon Willison's Weblog, Sept 23, 2026

Simon Willison discusses the latest AI fad, Jev, also known as "System One" models. "I'm with Maggie Appleton," he writes, "I think 'decision models' is a better name for these." Is basically black box AI. "Jev is an interesting variant on the usual LLM format: it still accepts text inputs, but instead of text output it returns floating point numbers corresponding to categories, yes/no questions, ratings, and associated confidence scores." As Willison notes, "It's great for anything that can be expressed as a classification task—think spam detection, suggesting labels, prioritization and ranking." Ah, that describes (sadly) so much educational activity (people have been going gaga over it in LinkedIn).
